analysis.one_liner: Extends the federal backstop for nuclear accident liability and adds worker-safety and security rules for plants and labs.
analysis.headline: The House passed it by voice vote in November 2001, but the Senate never brought it to a vote and it died when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The Price-Anderson system makes the federal government the insurer of last resort for nuclear accidents: plant operators and Department of Energy contractors carry a set amount of insurance, and the government covers liability above that, while a cap limits what the industry itself must pay. This bill would have extended that arrangement from 2002 to 2017 and set the government's indemnity for DOE contractors at $10 billion per incident. It also attached real public protections: for the first time, OSHA-equivalent health and safety rules for workers at DOE nuclear sites, the repeal of blanket civil-penalty exemptions enjoyed by universities and AT&T running national labs, new security checks for nuclear materials shipments, and post-9/11 security exercises for power plants.
analysis.who_benefits: Nuclear power plant operators and DOE contractors gain a 15-year extension of the federal liability backstop, capping their worst-case accident costs. Workers at DOE nuclear facilities gain OSHA-level safety protections they did not previously have. Potential victims of a nuclear incident keep a guaranteed federal compensation channel that was otherwise set to expire in 2002.

how_it_helps.text: Extends the federal indemnification authority for NRC licensees, DOE contractors, and nonprofit educational institutions from August 2002 to August 2017, keeping the nuclear accident compensation system in place.

Sets the government's indemnity for DOE contractors at $10 billion per incident above required financial protection, and raises coverage for incidents outside the U.S. from $100 million to $500 million.

Requires the Secretary of Energy to issue worker health and safety rules for DOE nuclear contractors that are substantially equivalent to OSHA's industrial and construction standards, with comparable civil penalties — protections these workers previously lacked.

Repeals blanket exemptions from DOE civil penalties that had been granted to the University of Chicago, the University of California, AT&T, Princeton, and others running national laboratories, and authorizes the Attorney General to recover federal indemnity payments caused by a contractor officer's intentional misconduct.

Adds post-9/11 security measures: manifests and federal background checks for nuclear materials shipments, a presidential study of threats to licensed plants, and periodic force-on-force security exercises at sensitive nuclear facilities.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers bear the exposure above what the industry pays, since the federal government indemnifies accident liability beyond the required insurance and the DOE contractor backstop is $10 billion per incident. The extension also keeps the Price-Anderson cap in place, which limits the total amount nuclear operators must pay for a catastrophic accident and channels accident costs away from full industry liability.

drawbacks.text: The core of the bill extends the government's role as nuclear insurer of last resort for 15 years, with a $10 billion indemnity per DOE incident and inflation adjustments at least every five years — putting public dollars behind the industry's worst-case liability.

Civil penalties for tax-exempt contractors like universities running national labs are capped at the discretionary fee the government pays them, so the new penalty rules bite far less on nonprofit contractors.
The Attorney General's financial-accountability clawback applies only to for-profit contractors and is capped at the profit the contractor derived from the contract.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill pairs a genuine public good — a functioning compensation system for nuclear accident victims and the first real OSHA-level safety rules for DOE nuclear site workers, plus tightened penalty rules and post-9/11 security requirements — with a continued federal subsidy in the form of the liability backstop. The worker-safety and penalty reforms are meaningful public gains; the 15-year extension of taxpayer exposure is the trade-off, and the bill's own structure (profit-capped clawbacks, fee-capped penalties for nonprofits) softens accountability even where it tightens it.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it by voice vote under a fast-track procedure in late November 2001, but the Senate only read it and placed it on its calendar — no senator ever voted on it before that Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Introduced October 2, 2001 by Rep. Heather Wilson, the bill moved quickly through the Energy and Commerce Committee, which reported it amended, and a short sequential referral to the Science Committee was discharged the next day.

On November 27, 2001, the House passed the bill by voice vote under suspension of the rules — a fast-track procedure that allows passage with no roll-call record and typically requires broad agreement.

The Senate received the bill on November 28, read it twice, and placed it on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders, where it remained with no floor action through the end of the 107th Congress on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: In the short run, the federal government kept the pre-2002 indemnification terms rather than taking on the expanded 15-year, $10 billion commitment this bill set. Nuclear operators and DOE contractors did not get the liability extension, but DOE site workers and nearby residents also did not get the new OSHA-equivalent safety rules, penalty reforms, and security measures the bill contained — a loss for the public side of the bargain.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo held; no new terms either way

sides.party_line_note: No roll-call votes were taken: the House passed it by voice vote under suspension of the rules and the Senate never voted, so the record shows no measurable partisan split on the bill itself.

industries.note: The bill extends the federal liability backstop to 2017 and modestly raises the industry's own deferred-premium obligation, keeping the government behind operators for catastrophic accident costs. Because the cap limits what operators must pay above their insurance and the taxpayer absorbs the rest, the industry's core interest here runs against full public protection, even though the bill's security provisions are meant to protect the public around the plants.

industries.industry: DOE national laboratory contractors (universities, AT&T, Battelle)
industries.note: Contractors gain a $10 billion federal indemnity per incident extended to 2017, but they lose their blanket exemptions from DOE civil penalties and must accept OSHA-equivalent worker safety rules with real fines. The bill's clawback for intentional misconduct applies to for-profit contractors, with nonprofits' penalties capped at their contract fee.
